blocks.title: ACT English — Practice Test 2
blocks.intro: Six essays, 50 questions, 35 minutes — the same length and timing as the English section of the enhanced ACT. questions.p:
**Passage I: The Smell of Semolina**

Every summer of my childhood, I spent my mornings in my grandmother's bakery in Alexandria, two streets back from the Corniche. The shop was small, __[1] it's__ walls lined with metal trays and its air thick with the smell of butter and semolina. My grandmother, Teta Samia, had opened it in 1979, and even at seventy she still arrived before dawn to light the ovens.

Teta never wrote down a single recipe. She measured flour with a chipped blue cup and judged the dough by the way it felt under her palms. "Bread tells you when it is ready," she would say, pressing a floury thumb into a loaf to show me how it sprang back. I tried to copy her, but my loaves came out either as flat as plates or as hard as stones. In addition, she never laughed at my failures; she simply handed me another lump of dough and told me to try again.

By the time I was twelve, I had learned the rhythm of the shop. At six o'clock, the first customers arrives: fishermen wanting warm rolls, schoolchildren counting coins for a slice of basbousa, and old men who came mostly to talk. Teta knew every one of them by name. She also knew which families could not pay that week, and she quietly let them take their bread anyway.

Last year, Teta decided it was time to retire, and the bakery was given by her to me. I was terrified. Without her beside me, I was sure the dough would refuse to rise. On my first morning alone, I stood in front of the ovens for a long time, lasting many long minutes, wondering whether I should simply lock the door and go home.

Then the bell above the door rang. It was Am Hassan, a fisherman who had bought rolls from Teta for forty years. He did not ask where she was. He just smiled, put a coin on the counter, and waited. I reached for the chipped blue cup, and my hands, it turned out, remembered everything.
questions.q: Question 1. Which choice is best for the underlined portion? (Choose NO CHANGE if the original is best.)
questions.e: The walls belong to the shop, so the possessive pronoun "its" (no apostrophe) is needed. "It's" means "it is" ("it is walls" makes no sense); "its'" is not a word; "their" is plural but the shop is singular.

**Passage II: Keepers of the Light**

For as long as people have sailed, they have needed a way to find the shore in the dark. The earliest guides were simple fires lit on hilltops near harbours. Over time, these fires were moved onto stone towers so that they could be seen from farther away. Sailors who saw the flames knew that rocks and shallow water __[11] was__ close and that they should steer with care.

The most famous early lighthouse stood in Alexandria. Built on the island of Pharos in the third century BCE, the tower's height was probably more than 100 metres, and a fire burned at its top. Ancient writers counted it among the Seven Wonders of the World. Over many centuries, earthquakes damaged the tower until it finally collapsed. In the 1470s, Sultan Qaitbay built a fortress on the same site, using some of the lighthouse's fallen stones.

For most of the two thousand years after Pharos was built, lighthouses changed very little: each one was still a tower with a fire or a group of candles burning at the top of it, high up. The light was weak, and much of it escaped uselessly into the sky. Then, in 1822, the French scientist Augustin Fresnel designed a new kind of lens. Instead of one thick piece of glass, his lens used rings of glass prisms that sparkled in the sunlight. A lamp placed behind a Fresnel lens could be seen by sailors many kilometres out at sea.

Lighthouses also needed people. For generations, keepers lived beside the towers, climbing the stairs each night to trim the wicks, polish the lenses, and they wound the clockwork that turned the light. The work was lonely and sometimes dangerous. In the twentieth century, however, electric lamps and automatic machines took over these tasks, and most keepers left there posts. Today, ships rely mainly on satellite navigation, yet many lighthouses still shine, both as a backup and as a reminder of the long human effort to keep sailors safe.
questions.q: Question 11. Which choice is best for the underlined portion? (Choose NO CHANGE if the original is best.)
questions.e: The subject "rocks and shallow water" is two things joined by "and", so it takes the plural "were"; the past tense matches "saw" and "knew". "Was", "has been" and "is" are all singular, and "is"/"has been" also shift the tense.

**Passage III: The Dance of the Honeybee**

When a honeybee finds a good patch of flowers, she does not keep the discovery to herself. She flies back to the hive and __[21] performs, a__ special movement known as the waggle dance. In the 1940s, the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch kind of proved that this dance works like a map.

The dancer runs in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run. The angle of the run shows the direction of the food in relation to the sun. **Passage IV: Give the Centre Back to People**

Walk through the centre of almost any large city at rush hour, and you will notice the same thing: cars. They block the roads, crowd the pavements where they park, and __[26] fills__ the air with noise and fumes. Drivers spend hours each week stuck in jams, while people on foot squeeze past bumpers. I believe that cities should ban private cars from their central districts. Doing so would make city centres cleaner and safer for the people who live and work there.

The first benefit is cleaner air. Traffic is one of the main sources of air pollution in cities; breathing polluted air for many years can damage a person's lungs and heart. Children and older people, whose bodies are more sensitive, suffer the most. When cars are removed from a district, the air there becomes noticeably cleaner.

Second, a car-free centre would be safer. Without heavy traffic, children could walk to school on their own, by themselves, and older people could cross the street without fear. Fewer cars also mean fewer accidents. Streets that were once dangerous could become places to play, sit, and meet. The Spanish city of Pontevedra closed most of its centre to private cars in 1999. Since then, the city has hosted several large festivals.

Critics argue that a ban would hurt shops, since customers could no longer drive to the door. However, shops on car-free streets often gain customers, because people on foot tend to stop, look in windows, and come back. A street full of walkers, not traffic, is good for business. Cities would also need to provide good buses and trams and also cheap ones too, as well as parking at the edge of the centre, so that no one is left without a way in.

City centres are built for people long before they were built for cars. Their squares, markets, and narrow lanes were designed for walking, talking, and trading, not for parking. It is time to give them back.

**Passage VI: Not What I Expected**

On my first morning as a volunteer at the wildlife rescue centre near Fayoum, I expected to spend the day cuddling baby animals. I had even brought my phone to take photos of them. Instead, the manager, a tall woman named Dr. Nadia, handed me a bucket and a __[41] brush, I__ spent the next two hours scrubbing empty cages.

"Clean cages stop infections," she explained when she saw my totally bummed-out face. "A sick animal cannot fight off germs the way a healthy one can." By lunchtime my arms ached, but I was beginning to understand. I had never thought of germs as an animal's enemy; now I knew why the work mattered.

In the afternoon, Dr. Nadia let me help with a real patient: a young kestrel that had been found tangled in fishing line. Their left wing was bandaged, and it watched us with fierce yellow eyes. My job was to hold a towel over its head while she checked the bandage. Its sharp talons, I noticed, were pulled tight against its body. "Birds stay calmer in the dark," she whispered. I held my breath, afraid that if I moved, the bird would panic.

The kestrel has been at the centre for three weeks. Dr. Nadia told me that its wing had almost healed and that, if all went well, the bird would be released the following month. Then she showed me a chart on the wall listing every animal in the centre: two foxes, a family of hedgehogs, a desert owl, and the kestrel. Each name had a release date written beside it. The goal, Dr. Nadia explained, was always to return every animal to the wild.

That evening, as I walked to the bus stop, I came to the realisation and understood that rescue work is not mainly about cuddling animals. It is about patience, cleanliness, and, finally, letting go. Me and my friend Karim have already signed up for every Saturday this summer. I want to be there when the kestrel flies free.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for **every** question, including the ones you got right — a lucky guess is not a skill yet.
Write a list of the questions you missed and the skill tag of each one: Production of Writing, Knowledge of Language, or Conventions of Standard English.
Look for patterns. Missed commas, semicolons, its/it's or verbs? Go back to "ACT Punctuation" and "Sentence Structure", plus "ACT Grammar and Usage".
Missed add/delete, writer's-goal or transition questions? Review "Relevance: Add, Delete and Writer's Goal" and "Organisation: Order and Transitions".
Missed questions about wordiness, tone or the precise word? Review "Concision and Redundancy" and "Word Choice and Tone".
Ran out of time? Reread "How to Attack ACT English" and practise answering as you read.
Wait a few days, then take ACT English — Practice Test 1 (or retake this one) under the same timed conditions.
